purpose: Independent practice of C1.3 — finding missing elements in different positions, extending in both directions, and justifying predictions using the rule.
student_learning_goal: I can find a missing animal and tell my partner why I am sure.

parts.answer_key: Strip A: cell 3 = Finn. Rule = AB. Wait — re-check. Strip A reads Bea-Finn-?-Bea-Finn-Bea. With AB rule (Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn-Bea-Finn), cell 3 should be Bea (not Finn). Cells 1=Bea, 2=Finn, 3=Bea, 4=Finn, 5=Bea — wait but the picture says cell 4=Bea, 5=Finn, 6=Bea. Let me re-check: pattern AB applied to 6 cells: Bea, Finn, Bea, Finn, Bea, Finn. So cells should be: 1=Bea, 2=Finn, 3=Bea, 4=Finn, 5=Bea, 6=Finn. The strip as described shows cells 1,2,4,5,6 = Bea, Finn, Bea, Finn, Bea. So 1=Bea, 2=Finn, 4=Bea, 5=Finn, 6=Bea. Cell 3 (missing) = Bea. Rule = AB. Correct answer: cell 3 = Bea, Rule = AB. Strip B: cells 1–5 = Bea, Finn, Finn, Bea, Finn. With ABB rule, full sequence is Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn. Cell 6 = Finn. Rule = ABB. Strip C: cells 2–6 = Finn, Bibi, Bea, Finn, Bibi. With ABC rule, full sequence is Bea-Finn-Bibi-Bea-Finn-Bibi. Cell 1 = Bea. Rule = ABC.

parts.answer_key: Rule = ABB. Full sequence: Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn. Wait — that's the rule running backwards from cell 3 (Bea). Let me think carefully. The rule is ABB where A=Bea, B=Finn. So the sequence is Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn. Cells 3–6 are given as Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea. So cell 3 starts a new core (Bea is the A). Working backward: cell 2 must be the LAST cell of the previous core, which is Finn. Cell 1 must be the SECOND-LAST of the previous core, also Finn. Working forward: cell 7 must be Finn, cell 8 must be Finn. Final: cell 1=Finn, cell 2=Finn, cells 3–6 as given (Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea), cell 7=Finn, cell 8=Finn. Full: Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn-Bea-Finn-Finn. Loop drawn around any consecutive Bea-Finn-Finn group. Sentence: 'The rule is ABB. I know cells 1 and 2 are Finn and Finn because the rule keeps repeating.'

parts.answer_key: Rule AAB means each core is two of one animal followed by one of another. With cell 5 = Bibi, multiple valid solutions exist depending on which letter (A or B) Bibi plays. The most natural reading: the cores end on B, so cell 5 (Bibi) is B in the second core. Cores would be: cells 1–3 = A-A-B, cells 4–6 = A-A-B. So cell 6 must be a NEW core's start (or be A starting again). Specifically: cells 1=A, 2=A, 3=B (Bibi), 4=A, 5=A, 6=B (Bibi). But then cell 5 is A not Bibi. Alternative: cell 5 = B, so the core boundaries fall between cells 3-4 and 6-7. Cells 1-3=AAB, cells 4-6=AAB, with cell 5 being the second A. That makes cell 5 = A, not B. The cleanest answer: cells 4=A, 5=A, 6=B with Bibi as A. Then cell 5 = Bibi (A), cell 6 = some other animal as B. Working backward: cell 3 = B, cells 1-2 = A-A. So sequence: A-A-B-A-A-B = e.g., Bibi-Bibi-Finn-Bibi-Bibi-Finn. Final: cells 1=Bibi, 2=Bibi, 3=Finn (or any non-Bibi), 4=Bibi, 5=Bibi (given), 6=Finn. Accept any valid AAB sequence with Bibi as the A and ANY other animal (Bea/Finn/Moss) as the B. Sentence: 'I am sure because the rule AAB needs two of one animal then one of another, so since cell 5 is Bibi I made Bibi the A.'

early_finisher_prompt: If you finish, flip the page over and draw a 10-cell parade with TWO missing cells anywhere — start, middle, end. Trade with a partner and let them be the detective.
teacher_notes: Lesson 4 consolidation. The most diagnostic part is Part 2 — backward extension is the new Grade 1 stretch. Children who fill cells 1 and 2 correctly without prompting are at L3 or L4 on C1.3. Children who only fill cells 7 and 8 (forward) and leave 1 and 2 empty need the conference. Part 3 is open-ended — accept any valid AAB sequence as long as cell 5 = Bibi and the rule holds. Use the sentence-frame answers as oral-justification proxies: a child who can complete the sentence in writing has internalized the justify habit. Children who write only the rule label without explaining 'because' need a follow-up conference.
